title: The Case of the Overdue Twenty
story: Twenty books from Ms. Ortiz's class showed overdue on March 17. The library had changed its loan period from fourteen days to twenty-one on March 1. Her class checked the books out on March 2, and every printed slip reads March 23. The catalog listed all twenty as due March 16. A power cut on March 10 shut the system down for most of a day. Staff rebuilt the catalog from a backup copy made on February 26. The new twenty-one-day rule was entered into the system on March 1. Nothing borrowed after March 11 has shown overdue at all. No librarian edited a due date, and the log confirms it. The slips and the catalog disagree by exactly seven days.
question: Why does the catalog call the twenty books overdue?

suspects.why: staff rebuilt the catalog from a backup copy made on February 26
nothing borrowed after March 11 has shown overdue at all
no librarian edited a due date, and the log confirms it
every printed slip reads March 23

answer: The rebuilt catalog is running the old fourteen-day rule.
proof: “Staff rebuilt the catalog from a backup copy made on February 26.”
“The new twenty-one-day rule was entered into the system on March 1.”
clears: The power cut: “Nothing borrowed after March 11 has shown overdue at all.”
A librarian: “No librarian edited a due date, and the log confirms it.”
The class: “every printed slip reads March 23.”
explain: Everything in the story happened. The order is what settles it: the backup was made on February 26 and the new rule went in on March 1, so the copy staff restored had never heard of the twenty-one-day loan. The books are due March 23, exactly as the slips say.
